clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous group of autosomal recessive disorders defined by a quantitative reduction in mitochondrial DNA copy number in affected tissues, causing multiple respiratory-chain enzyme deficiencies.
Caused by defects in nuclear genes that maintain mtDNA replication or the mitochondrial nucleotide pool, including POLG, TWNK, TK2, DGUOK, MPV17, SUCLA2, SUCLG1, RRM2B and TYMP.
Clinical forms are grouped as myopathic (TK2), encephalomyopathic (SUCLA2, SUCLG1, RRM2B), hepatocerebral (DGUOK, MPV17, POLG, TWNK) and neurogastrointestinal (TYMP, causing MNGIE).
Because complex II is entirely nuclear-encoded it is typically spared, whereas complexes I, III and IV that contain mtDNA-encoded subunits are deficient, a useful biochemical clue.
Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome (POLG) combines intractable epilepsy, developmental regression and liver failure; valproate can precipitate fatal hepatotoxicity and should be avoided.
MNGIE (thymidine phosphorylase deficiency) features ptosis, external ophthalmoplegia, severe gastrointestinal dysmotility with cachexia, peripheral neuropathy and leukoencephalopathy.
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced mtDNA content in muscle or liver alongside targeted gene or panel testing; the encephalomyopathic SUCLA2 and SUCLG1 forms show mild methylmalonic aciduria.
Management is largely supportive, but TK2 deficiency may respond to nucleoside or nucleotide substitution and MNGIE to therapies that lower circulating thymidine.
reference.pathophysiology: Faithful maintenance of the mitochondrial genome depends on nuclear-encoded replication machinery, including the polymerase POLG and the TWNK helicase, and on a balanced supply of deoxyribonucleotides delivered by mitochondrial salvage and cytosolic pathways involving TK2, DGUOK, RRM2B, TYMP and SUCLA2/SUCLG1, with MPV17 supporting nucleotide homeostasis. Pathogenic variants either cripple mtDNA replication directly or distort the mitochondrial deoxyribonucleotide pool, leading to a progressive fall in mtDNA copy number. Because several essential respiratory-chain subunits are mtDNA-encoded, depletion produces a combined deficiency of complexes I, III, IV and V with relative preservation of the wholly nuclear-encoded complex II, impairing oxidative phosphorylation in the most energy-dependent tissues such as brain, muscle, liver and gut. The specific gene defect and the tissues in which depletion is most severe determine the clinical subtype.
additionalDifferentials: Primary mtDNA point-mutation or deletion syndromes (Leigh, MELAS, Kearns-Sayre)
Other nuclear respiratory-chain assembly or subunit defects
Congenital myopathies and spinal muscular atrophy for the myopathic form
Neonatal or infantile liver failure of other cause (tyrosinaemia, galactosaemia, viral hepatitis)
Organic acidaemias, especially methylmalonic aciduria mimicking SUCLA2/SUCLG1 disease
Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction of other cause for MNGIE
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative mtDNA content (copy number) in muscle or liver
Respiratory-chain enzyme assays showing combined complex I, III and IV deficiency
Nuclear gene panel or exome for mtDNA-maintenance genes
Blood and CSF lactate, plasma amino acids and urine organic acids including methylmalonate
Plasma thymidine and deoxyuridine when MNGIE is suspected
Liver function and synthetic tests, with muscle biopsy and histochemistry
Brain MRI and nerve conduction studies as the phenotype dictates
redFlags: Rapidly progressive infantile liver failure with encephalopathy
Intractable seizures or status epilepticus with regression (Alpers-POLG)
Progressive respiratory muscle weakness and ventilatory failure (TK2)
Exposure to valproate in a child with possible POLG-related disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies by subtype and gene: hepatocerebral and severe myopathic forms are frequently fatal in infancy or early childhood, whereas some presentations, including certain TK2 and later-onset forms, survive longer and are increasingly influenced by emerging targeted therapies.
pitfalls: Giving valproate for seizures before excluding POLG-related disease, risking fatal liver failure.
Relying on blood mtDNA levels, which may be normal despite marked tissue depletion.
Overlooking the sparing of complex II as a diagnostic pointer.
Missing the mild methylmalonic aciduria that flags SUCLA2 and SUCLG1 forms.
Attributing MNGIE cachexia to a primary gastrointestinal disorder and delaying metabolic work-up.
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
management: For TK2-related myopathic disease use nucleoside/nucleotide substrate therapy with deoxycytidine and deoxythymidine as an emerging targeted treatment
Avoid mitochondrial toxins, critically avoiding sodium valproate in POLG-related Alpers-Huttenlocher disease because it can precipitate fatal hepatotoxicity, and use aminoglycosides cautiously

In MNGIE from thymidine phosphorylase deficiency, consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell or liver transplantation to restore enzyme activity, with aggressive, often parenteral, nutritional support for dysmotility and cachexia
Provide supportive care for epilepsy, nutrition and mobility, using non-hepatotoxic anticonvulsants and mitochondrial cofactors such as coenzyme Q10 and riboflavin
Consider liver transplantation selectively in hepatocerebral forms, weighing any neurological involvement
Monitor for progressive hepatic, neurological, gastrointestinal and cardiac decline
Offer genetic counselling for these autosomal recessive disorders with family testing
Coordinate multidisciplinary specialist care across metabolic medicine, neurology and hepatology
